title: Playing golf on the Grand Strand

sections.h: A lot of courses, and no single best one
p: Visit Myrtle Beach puts the number at about 90 courses on the Grand Strand. Other sources count fewer, mostly because they draw the boundaries differently, so treat any exact figure as rough. The point is that you will never run out of tee times to look at, and the sheer choice can be paralyzing.

We list 16 courses here. That's a starting sample, not the full field, picked to show the range: resort courses with famous names, public courses that take walk-ons and a few that have hosted real tournaments.

Think about who is playing. The four courses at Barefoot Resort were designed by Dye, Norman, Love and Fazio, which makes them an easy way to compare big-name architects in one trip. Myrtle Beach National's King's North is an Arnold Palmer redesign from 1996 that reopened after a long renovation. TPC Myrtle Beach is a Tom Fazio design where wetlands come into play on a lot of holes. Pawleys Plantation and Wachesaw East sit toward the Murrells Inlet and Pawleys Island end of the Strand, a bit calmer than the traffic around Myrtle Beach.
If you're traveling with a mixed group, ask whether a course has a short set of tees. A shorter tee box can turn a frustrating round into a fun one for newer players.

Golf sites generally call March through May and September through November the best weather. Winter is the least crowded and often the best value, and January and February are usually the cheapest time to book. Summer works well if the beach is the main event and golf is a morning or evening extra. Plan on early tee times when it is hot.

list: Prices and tee times change by day and season, and they are often better when booked directly or through a package. Check the course's own page.
Ask about cart policy, dress code and whether the course has been renovated recently. A few of the well-known layouts have been closed for work.
Spring and fall weekends go first. If your dates are fixed, book earlier.
